amendments.why: PSA.133.1 met a case rule 52 had not considered: an infinitive construct with an overt subject and no preposition on it, rendered *For brethren to dwell*. Rule 52's closing paragraph already gives the bare *to* to the infinitive on the ground that English writes no bare infinitive complement, but it says nothing about the *for* English requires before such a clause's overt subject, and the two rules within reach decide it wrongly and in opposite directions: rule 33 would hand the word to `achim` as a bare nominal standing in the clause, and rule 55 would mark it `added` as a supplied subordinator. Neither fits - being the subject of an infinitive is not a case-function, exactly as rule 16 says of a topicalized nominal's fronting, and no finite clause stands for a subordinator to reach - so the verse pass had to reason the boundary out from scratch, and the next chapter to meet the construction would have had to do it again or guess. The amendment extends rule 52's own reasoning to the frame's opening word, names both competing rules by number so the ruling cannot be read as reaching past them, and closes by leaving rule 25's anticipatory *it* outside the unit, so that widening the frame cannot draw a supplied matrix subject in with it. The condition is narrow: an overt subject, no preposition on the infinitive, and the *for ... to* frame actually written; where a `le-` stands the existing sentences govern first. Nothing in the corpus tables supplied contradicts it, and the corpus was silent on the construction rather than against it. Every other sentence of rule 52 is returned unchanged.
amendments.rule: **A purpose `לְ` + infinitive construct recast as a finite clause gives the complementizer to the preposition and the supplied subject and modal to the infinitive.** The ASV writes *that men may bring*, *that I may be glorified*. This is rule 48's division outside the privative `מִן`, and for the same reason: the complementizer is what the preposition contributes, while a supplied subject pronoun and a separately written modal belong to the verb, as rule 17 keeps a subject pronoun with its verb. The corpus puts the *that* on the preposition in 28 units across 17 chapters and never on the infinitive, so this too is settled. Where the ASV writes no English word at all for the preposition there is nothing to place, and the `לְ` goes `unrepresented` under rule 40. **Read that as no word, not as no complementizer.** The complementizer is what a finite recasting spends on the preposition, but a recasting that makes the infinitive an English gerund or a bare verbal noun writes an ordinary preposition in that same position, and that word is the `לְ`'s on the same terms: `לִשְׁמֹר אֶת־בְּרִיתוֹ` → *by keeping his covenant*, `לִשְׁלֹחַ מַלְאָכָיו` → *in sending his ambassadors*, `לְהָפֵר בְּרִית` → *by breaking the covenant*, `לָצֶקֶת` → *for casting*, `לֶאֱכֹל` → *an end of eating*. The corpus aligns a `לְ` before an infinitive construct to a written *to* in 583 units, to *that* in 81, and to *for*, *in*, *of*, *by*, *after* or *when* in 53 more, against 527 marked `unrepresented`; the two groups do not disagree, because every unrepresented one is a recasting that writes no function word at all — *left off building*, *the building of the house*. So ask whether a word is written before reaching for rule 40, and do not read the gerund itself as the recasting that silences the preposition. **Where two such `לְ` + infinitive phrases stand in one clause and the ASV writes one complementizer and one preposition, count them as this rule's last sentence directs rather than taking them in linear order.** `לִשְׁמֹר אֶת־בְּרִיתוֹ לְעָמְדָהּ` → *that by keeping his covenant it might stand* gives *by* to the `לְ` of the gerund and *that* to the `לְ` whose infinitive the finite clause renders: the ASV fronts the complementizer ahead of the gerund adjunct, and that reordering says nothing about which preposition it answers to. **A temporal preposition before an infinitive construct is read the same way.** Where `בְּ` or `כְּ` + infinitive is recast as a finite temporal clause — `בְּחֻמָּם` → *When they are heated*, `בְּלֶכְתּוֹ` → *when he went*, `כְּבֹאֲךָ` → *When thou comest*, `כְּכַלֹּתְךָ` → *when thou hast made an end* — the preposition takes the *when*, the infinitive keeps the verb, and the suffix takes the subject pronoun the ASV writes for it under rule 18. The corpus aligns `בְּ` to *when* in 45 units, so the temporal case is settled on the same footing as the purpose case. Read the preposition that is present rather than its lemma: a `לְ` heading such a phrase goes the same way even where its object is the noun rather than the infinitive, as in `לְקוֹל תִּתּוֹ` → *When he uttereth his voice*. **But only a preposition that still has an English word to take can take it.** Where no preposition is present and the construct relation itself is what the English *when* realizes, rule 19 puts that word on the *nomen rectum*, which is the infinitive: `עֵת הִדְרִיכָהּ` → *at the time when it is trodden* gives *at the time* to `עֵת` and *when ... is trodden* to the infinitive. **And a preposition on which the ASV has already spent its own English word is in the same position as an absent one.** Where the preposition heads a construct noun, the ASV writes a word for that preposition and a second temporal word besides, the second answers to the construct relation and not to the preposition, so rule 19 puts it on the *nomen rectum*: `בְּיוֹם הֵעָשׂוֹתוֹ` → *in the day when they shall make it* gives *in* to the `בְּ` and *the day* to `יוֹם`, leaving *when they shall make* to the infinitive, whose own suffix takes the pronoun rule 18 gives it. Count the ASV's function words against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s and rule 29 counts the ASV's *the*s: a preposition holding an English word of its own is not a home for a second one, and giving it both would leave the construct's relation unrendered against rule 2. **But that count places the second word on a morpheme that is there to take it, and a noun the projection writes as an absolute has no rectum standing under it.** Where the preposition heads a noun MACULA tags absolute — as it does where a finite clause rather than an infinitive construct or another nominal follows the noun — no construct relation is written in the phrase at all, so rule 19 has nothing to place the second temporal word on: that word answers to no morpheme in the clause and is its own `added` unit under rule 55, while the preposition and the noun each keep the English written for them. `בְּיוֹם קָרָאתִי` → *In* ***the day*** ***that*** *I called* gives *In* to the `בְּ` and *the day* to `יוֹם`, the determiner supplied under rule 15, leaves *I called* to the finite verb, and marks the *that* `added`. Read MACULA's morphology rather than the pointing, exactly as rule 29 directs, and read what stands under the noun: an infinitive construct or another nominal under a construct noun is a rectum and the preceding sentences govern, and a finite clause under an absolute noun is not one. Rule 46 does not reach such a word either, since the noun the ASV writes before the clause is a written antecedent and that rule's headless case governs a clause with none. And where an apodosis follows whose waw the ASV leaves unrendered, that waw is `unrepresented` under rule 14 and is not a home for the supplied word, which stands ahead of the temporal clause rather than at the apodosis's head, exactly as rule 45 reads a *that* written inside its frame. **Where no preposition stands before the infinitive construct at all, the English infinitive marker *to* belongs to the infinitive's own unit and is never `added`.** English writes no bare infinitive complement, so that word is what the infinitive itself licenses, exactly as rule 15 gives a supplied *a* to the noun that licenses it and rule 46 gives a supplied *them that* to a bare participle: `מֵאֵן בִּלְעָם הֲלֹךְ עִמָּנוּ` → *Balaam refuseth* ***to come*** *with us* and `הֲיָכוֹל אוּכַל דַּבֵּר מְאוּמָה` → *have I now any power at all* ***to speak*** *anything* each give the *to* to the infinitive, headed on the lexical verb under rule 24. Read whether a preposition is present before reaching for this sentence, since one and the same infinitive is read both ways in one chapter: `לַהֲלֹךְ עִמָּכֶם` → *to go with you* gives the written *to* to the `לְ` and only *go* to `הֲלֹךְ`, while the bare `הֲלֹךְ` above holds both words. And this reaches only a *to* the ASV has written: a modal's bare complement — *cannot go beyond* — has none to place, and a preposition the recasting leaves unrendered is `unrepresented` under rule 40 as before. **And an infinitive construct with an overt subject takes the whole *for … to* frame the English clause requires.** English writes no infinitival clause with an overt subject without a complementizing *for* standing before that subject, so where the Hebrew writes a subject for a preposition-less infinitive construct and the ASV renders the pair as *for X to V*, both words are what the infinitive itself licenses on exactly the terms of the preceding sentences: they belong to that infinitive's one discontinuous unit under rule 25, wrapped around the subject, which keeps only its own English, and neither is `added`. `שֶׁבֶת אַחִים` → ***For*** *brethren* ***to dwell*** gives *For to dwell* to `שֶׁבֶת` and *brethren* to `אָח`, headed on the lexical verb under rule 24. Do not give the *for* to the subject noun under rule 33: what that rule places is a word stating what a bare nominal's own case-function contributes to its clause, and standing as the subject of an infinitive is not such a case-function, exactly as rule 16 says of a topicalized nominal's fronting. Do not mark it `added` under rule 55 either, since that rule governs a subordinator the ASV has written over a clause the Hebrew writes finite, and here the word is part of the frame the ASV's own infinitival recasting requires. Test by subtraction as elsewhere — drop the *for* and ask whether a nominal has lost the relation it bears to its clause, or whether the infinitival clause the ASV built has been left ungrammatical. Two limits. Where a preposition stands on the infinitive it takes the ASV's word first, on the terms above, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied reading does. And an anticipatory *it* the ASV writes in the matrix clause for such an extraposed infinitival subject is no part of the frame: it is rule 25's expletive and is its own `added` unit, while the matrix predicate keeps the copula rule 20 gives it. **And the verb that takes such a bare *to* need not be an infinitive in the Hebrew.** Where a second Hebrew verb of any form — an imperative, a perfect, an imperfect — stands with no preposition on it and the ASV subordinates it to a governing verb as an English infinitive complement, the written *to* is what that English infinitive licenses and it joins the subordinated verb's own unit, headed on the lexical verb under rule 24, exactly as the bare `הֲלֹךְ` above holds it: `מַהֵר עֲנֵנִי` → *Make haste* ***to answer*** *me* gives *to answer* to `עָנָה` and *Make haste* to `מַהֵר`, and `אֵלֶיךָ כִסִּתִי` → *I flee unto thee* ***to hide*** *me* gives *to hide me* to `כָּסָה`. Read what the ASV made of the verb rather than what MACULA tags it, exactly as rule 19 reads a participle or infinitive the ASV has written as an English verb and rule 33 defers only to a governing verb the ASV has itself rendered as one. Do not give such a *to* to the governing verb: a verb already holding an English word of its own is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, and rule 44's supplied-preposition clause places a preposition the English verb's valency needs to reach its own object, which a complementizing *to* standing before a second verb is not. Two limits. Where a preposition morpheme does stand before that verb it takes the word first, on the terms above, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied reading does. And where the governing verb and the subordinated verb are one and the same morpheme — a causative or other verb the ASV renders by a light verb and a second verb, as `הַשְׁמִיעֵנִי` → *Cause me* ***to hear*** and `הוֹשִׁיבַנִי` → *hath made me* ***to dwell*** — rule 44 keeps the whole phrase in that morpheme's one unit, headed on the lexical complement, and there is nothing to allocate.

And where an apodosis follows whose waw the ASV leaves unrendered, that waw is `unrepresented` under rule 14 and is not a home for the supplied word, which stands ahead of the temporal clause rather than at the apodosis's head, exactly as rule 45 reads a *that* written inside its frame. **Where no preposition stands before the infinitive construct at all, the English infinitive marker *to* belongs to the infinitive's own unit and is never `added`.** English writes no bare infinitive complement, so that word is what the infinitive itself licenses, exactly as rule 15 gives a supplied *a* to the noun that licenses it and rule 46 gives a supplied *them that* to a bare participle: `מֵאֵן בִּלְעָם הֲלֹךְ עִמָּנוּ` → *Balaam refuseth* ***to come*** *with us* and `הֲיָכוֹל אוּכַל דַּבֵּר מְאוּמָה` → *have I now any power at all* ***to speak*** *anything* each give the *to* to the infinitive, headed on the lexical verb under rule 24. Read whether a preposition is present before reaching for this sentence, since one and the same infinitive is read both ways in one chapter: `לַהֲלֹךְ עִמָּכֶם` → *to go with you* gives the written *to* to the `לְ` and only *go* to `הֲלֹךְ`, while the bare `הֲלֹךְ` above holds both words. And this reaches only a *to* the ASV has written: a modal's bare complement — *cannot go beyond* — has none to place, and a preposition the recasting leaves unrendered is `unrepresented` under rule 40 as before. **And an infinitive construct with an overt subject takes the whole *for … to* frame the English clause requires.** English writes no infinitival clause with an overt subject without a complementizing *for* standing before that subject, so where the Hebrew writes a subject for a preposition-less infinitive construct and the ASV renders the pair as *for X to V*, both words are what the infinitive itself licenses on exactly the terms of the preceding sentences: they belong to that infinitive's one discontinuous unit under rule 25, wrapped around the subject, which keeps only its own English, and neither is `added`. `שֶׁבֶת אַחִים` → ***For*** *brethren* ***to dwell*** gives *For to dwell* to `שֶׁבֶת` and *brethren* to `אָח`, headed on the lexical verb under rule 24. Do not give the *for* to the subject noun under rule 33: what that rule places is a word stating what a bare nominal's own case-function contributes to its clause, and standing as the subject of an infinitive is not such a case-function, exactly as rule 16 says of a topicalized nominal's fronting. Do not mark it `added` under rule 55 either, since that rule governs a subordinator the ASV has written over a clause the Hebrew writes finite, and here the word is part of the frame the ASV's own infinitival recasting requires. Test by subtraction as elsewhere — drop the *for* and ask whether a nominal has lost the relation it bears to its clause, or whether the infinitival clause the ASV built has been left ungrammatical. Two limits. Where a preposition stands on the infinitive it takes the ASV's word first, on the terms above, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied reading does. And an anticipatory *it* the ASV writes in the matrix clause for such an extraposed infinitival subject is no part of the frame: it is rule 25's expletive and is its own `added` unit, while the matrix predicate keeps the copula rule 20 gives it. **And the verb that takes such a bare *to* need not be an infinitive in the Hebrew.** Where a second Hebrew verb of any form — an imperative, a perfect, an imperfect — stands with no preposition on it and the ASV subordinates it to a governing verb as an English infinitive complement, the written *to* is what that English infinitive licenses and it joins the subordinated verb's own unit, headed on the lexical verb under rule 24, exactly as the bare `הֲלֹךְ` above holds it: `מַהֵר עֲנֵנִי` → *Make haste* ***to answer*** *me* gives *to answer* to `עָנָה` and *Make haste* to `מַהֵר`, and `אֵלֶיךָ כִסִּתִי` → *I flee unto thee* ***to hide*** *me* gives *to hide me* to `כָּסָה`. Read what the ASV made of the verb rather than what MACULA tags it, exactly as rule 19 reads a participle or infinitive the ASV has written as an English verb and rule 33 defers only to a governing verb the ASV has itself rendered as one. Do not give such a *to* to the governing verb: a verb already holding an English word of its own is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, and rule 44's supplied-preposition clause places a preposition the English verb's valency needs to reach its own object, which a complementizing *to* standing before a second verb is not. Two limits. Where a preposition morpheme does stand before that verb it takes the word first, on the terms above, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied reading does. And where the governing verb and the subordinated verb are one and the same morpheme — a causative or other verb the ASV renders by a light verb and a second verb, as `הַשְׁמִיעֵנִי` → *Cause me* ***to hear*** and `הוֹשִׁיבַנִי` → *hath made me* ***to dwell*** — rule 44 keeps the whole phrase in that morpheme's one unit, headed on the lexical complement, and there is nothing to allocate.
amended.why: PSA.133.1 met a case rule 52 had not considered: an infinitive construct with an overt subject and no preposition on it, rendered *For brethren to dwell*. Rule 52's closing paragraph already gives the bare *to* to the infinitive on the ground that English writes no bare infinitive complement, but it says nothing about the *for* English requires before such a clause's overt subject, and the two rules within reach decide it wrongly and in opposite directions: rule 33 would hand the word to `achim` as a bare nominal standing in the clause, and rule 55 would mark it `added` as a supplied subordinator. Neither fits - being the subject of an infinitive is not a case-function, exactly as rule 16 says of a topicalized nominal's fronting, and no finite clause stands for a subordinator to reach - so the verse pass had to reason the boundary out from scratch, and the next chapter to meet the construction would have had to do it again or guess. The amendment extends rule 52's own reasoning to the frame's opening word, names both competing rules by number so the ruling cannot be read as reaching past them, and closes by leaving rule 25's anticipatory *it* outside the unit, so that widening the frame cannot draw a supplied matrix subject in with it. The condition is narrow: an overt subject, no preposition on the infinitive, and the *for ... to* frame actually written; where a `le-` stands the existing sentences govern first. Nothing in the corpus tables supplied contradicts it, and the corpus was silent on the construction rather than against it. Every other sentence of rule 52 is returned unchanged.

report: Cross-verse check: none of the four candidate lemmas is a split. The article takes a written *the* at PSA.133.2 s002, s007, s011 and PSA.133.3 s014, and is `unrepresented` where the ASV writes none - PSA.133.1 s002 and PSA.133.3 s018 under rule 29's last sentence, PSA.133.2 s004 as rule 47's repeated agreement article. The difference lies in the ASV's determiners, not in the analysis.

The three participles of `yarad` are all recast as relative clauses, and the one difference that matters is whether a relative morpheme is written: PSA.133.2 s009 is bare and takes the supplied *That* into its own unit under rule 41 (all four of that rule's marks of predication were checked and none is present), while PSA.133.2 s016 and PSA.133.3 s005 stand under a written `she-` that takes the *That* under rule 46's first rider. *down* stays with the verb in all three under rule 44, and all three head on the lexical verb. *ran / came / cometh* is tense, not analysis.

`tov` is a predicate *good* in v1 and an attributive *precious* in v2, both attested in the corpus (*precious* at ECC.7.1 among them). `ke-` takes the construction's copula as *is like* in v2, where the preposition heads the clause's predicate under rule 49, and is a bare *Like* in v3, where the ASV writes no copula. Both are licensed by what the ASV wrote.

Read the dump end to end for the `added` units the lemma table cannot see. There are four, and they divide on stated grounds: the anticipatory *it* of v1, filling the subject slot for the extraposed infinitival subject under rule 25's expletive sentences; the referential *It* of v2, whose antecedent stands in the previous verse, so rule 10 leaves no morpheme in this verse to carry it; and the appositional *Even* of v2 and of v3, neither standing on a phrase a marker marks - v3 is rule 16's EZK.4.5 division exactly, the clause's one marker standing on `ha-berakhah`, which the ASV renders bare. No supplied subject pronoun is folded into a predicate to avoid the mark, and no *Even* reaches across the clause for a marker.

Construct chains are handled uniformly: where no article morpheme stands, the construct takes a supplied *the* (PSA.133.2 s018, PSA.133.3 s002, s007) and the rectum takes the chain's *of* under rule 19; PSA.133.1 differs only because an article morpheme does stand on the rectum while the ASV writes no *the* at all, which rule 29's last sentence marks `unrepresented` with the *A* going to the construct under rule 15. PSA.133.2's `zeqan aharon` is rule 29's possessive recasting, the name holding the whole possessive expression.

BSB: none of the three disagreements is a genuine error. `gam` (v1) is the emphatic particle BSB attaches to its phrase; the ASV's *together in unity* opens with `yachad`'s own ordinary word, so nothing is left for `gam` to own, and the nearest alternative - a rule 30 fusion of the pair - is already weighed in that unit's note. v2.004 is rule 47's agreement article, and v3.018 stands where the ASV writes *for evermore* with no *the*. All three are the documented convention difference and no accepted edge was changed for them.

Conventions: none recorded. The three notes the report flags as repeating - *Article with its written the*, *Preposition rendered upon*, *Written relative morpheme taking the ASV's That* - restate rules 15/29, 11 and 46 word for word, and the contract already binds every verse. Logging them would bury the one judgment that is genuinely chapter-scoped, and there is no such judgment here: v1's allocation of the single copula to the nearer of two coordinated predicates occurs once and is already documented in that unit's note with its competing reading named.

One amendment, to rule 52. PSA.133.1 renders a preposition-less infinitive construct with an overt subject as *For brethren to dwell*; rule 52 places the bare *to* but not the *for*, and the two rules within reach decide it wrongly and in opposite directions (rule 33 would give the word to the subject noun, rule 55 would mark it `added`). The amendment widens rule 52's own closing paragraph to the whole *for ... to* frame and states the boundary against both, keeping rule 25's anticipatory *it* outside the unit.
